This page outlines what you should set up and review before the Nextflow workshop begins if you **do not** have an NCSU Hazel HPC account. You'll need access to **your own HPC or compute environment** with Nextflow installed and the workshop's tools available, either as pre-installed software/modules or as containers.

## Install Nextflow on Your HPC

- [ ] Nextflow requires Java 17–21. Check whether Java is already available:

```bash
$ java -version
```

If it isn't, load or install it (e.g. `module avail java` on many HPC systems) before installing Nextflow.

- [ ] Check whether Nextflow is already available as an environment module on your HPC:

```bash
$ module avail nextflow
```

If it is, you can simply `module load nextflow` and skip the manual install below.

- [ ] Install Nextflow by following the [official installation instructions](https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/install.html). The simplest approach is:

```bash
$ curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash
```

This creates a `nextflow` executable in your current directory. Move it into a directory on your `$PATH` (e.g. `~/bin`) so it can be run from anywhere:

```bash
$ mkdir -p ~/bin
$ mv nextflow ~/bin/
$ export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin"
```

Add the `export PATH` line to your `~/.bashrc` (or equivalent) so it persists across logins.

- [ ] Confirm Nextflow runs:

```bash
$ nextflow -version
```

## Access to the Workshop's Tools

The workshop's exercises run a small number of common bioinformatics tools (e.g. **FastQC** and **Trimmomatic**) inside Nextflow processes. On Hazel, these are provided by the BRC as pre-built modules/containers (see [Loading BRC Modules](loading_brc_modules.qmd)) — outside NCSU, you'll need to provide equivalent access on your own system, using **one** of the following options.

### Option A: Pre-installed software or environment modules

- [ ] Check whether your HPC already provides these tools as environment modules or pre-installed software:

```bash
$ module avail fastqc
$ module avail trimmomatic
```

If they're available, note the `module load` command (or install path) for each — you'll substitute it for the BRC `module` directives used in the workshop's example pipelines.

### Option B: Containers via Singularity/Apptainer and BioContainers

If the tools aren't available as modules, you can run them from containers instead. [BioContainers](https://biocontainers.pro/) publishes ready-made container images for most common bioinformatics tools, built directly from their [Bioconda](https://bioconda.github.io/) packages.

- [ ] Check that a container engine is available on your HPC:

```bash
$ singularity --version
# or
$ apptainer --version
```

(Apptainer is the actively maintained successor to Singularity; the commands are interchangeable for our purposes.) If neither is installed, ask your HPC administrators — most institutional HPC systems provide one or the other as a module.

- [ ] Find the tool you need on BioContainers. Search for it at [biocontainers.pro](https://biocontainers.pro/) or browse its images directly on [quay.io/organization/biocontainers](https://quay.io/organization/biocontainers), and note the exact image tag (tool version + build hash), e.g. `fastqc:0.12.1--hdfd78af_0`.

- [ ] Pull the container image with `singularity pull` (or `apptainer pull`):

```bash
$ singularity pull fastqc.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/fastqc:0.12.1--hdfd78af_0
$ singularity pull trimmomatic.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/trimmomatic:0.39--hdfd78af_1
```

::: {.callout-note}
The workshop's example pipeline scripts request tools with a `module` directive, e.g. `module 'fastqc/0.12.1'`, which points Nextflow at a Hazel/BRC module. Outside Hazel, replace this with a `container` directive pointing at your `.sif` file (or the `docker://` image URI directly), and enable Singularity in your `nextflow.config`:

```groovy
singularity.enabled = true

process {
    withName: fastqc {
        container = '/path/to/fastqc.sif'
    }
    withName: trim {
        container = '/path/to/trimmomatic.sif'
    }
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
You don't have to pre-pull images by hand — if `singularity.enabled = true` and a process's `container` directive points at a `docker://` URI, Nextflow will pull and cache the image automatically the first time that process runs.
:::
